items.stem: Which test shows the presence of water?
options: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue
items.answer: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue
items.markingKey: Water hydrates CuSO₄ (white → blue) or anhydrous CoCl₂ (blue → pink).

items.stem: Explain why a positive result with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate does not show that water is pure.
items.answer: It tests for the presence of water only; impure water containing dissolved substances also turns it blue. Purity is shown by b.p. 100 °C/m.p. 0 °C.

items.stem: Explain how nitrates from fertilisers can cause fish in a lake to die.
items.answer: Nitrates cause rapid growth of algae (eutrophication); the algae die and are decomposed by bacteria, which use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark algal growth; 1 mark decomposition by bacteria; 1 mark oxygen depletion [3]

items.stem: Describe a chemical test to show that a liquid condensed from a candle flame contains water, and a physical test to find out whether it is pure water. Predict the results.
items.answer: Add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: turns white → blue (or cobalt(II) chloride blue → pink). Measure the boiling point: pure water boils at exactly 100 °C; this sample would be expected to do so if uncontaminated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark chemical test; 1 mark result; 1 mark boiling/melting point test; 1 mark expected result [4]

items.stem: Describe a chemical test to show that a liquid produced when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated contains water, and a physical test to find out whether it is pure water. Predict the results.
items.answer: Add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: turns white → blue (or cobalt(II) chloride blue → pink). Measure the boiling point: pure water boils at exactly 100 °C; this sample would be expected to do so if uncontaminated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark chemical test; 1 mark result; 1 mark boiling/melting point test; 1 mark expected result [4]

items.stem: A village gets its water from a lake. Algae have covered much of the lake surface this summer and some fish have died. (a) Describe a chemical test for water. (b) Name two pollutants that might be found in the river and their sources.
items.answer: (a) Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns white to blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride blue to pink). (b) Nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers; sewage from the town; metal compounds from industry; plastics from litter.

items.stem: Which physical test shows that a sample of water is pure?
options: It turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue
items.answer: It boils at exactly 100 °C
items.markingKey: Pure water: b.p. 100 °C and m.p. 0 °C at standard pressure.

items.stem: Explain why water from rivers is filtered before it is chlorinated.
items.answer: Filtration removes insoluble solids; otherwise solids could shelter microbes and use up chlorine.

items.stem: Some substances in river water are beneficial. Give one example and explain why.
items.answer: Dissolved oxygen for aquatic life, or some metal compounds/minerals such as calcium compounds for healthy teeth and bones.

items.stem: Describe a chemical test to show that a colourless liquid from a car radiator contains water, and a physical test to find out whether it is pure water. Predict the results.
items.answer: Add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: turns white → blue (or cobalt(II) chloride blue → pink). Measure the boiling point: pure water boils at exactly 100 °C; this sample would boil above 100 °C (and over a range) because it is impure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark chemical test; 1 mark result; 1 mark boiling/melting point test; 1 mark expected result [4]

items.stem: A water company in Jakarta takes water from a river that flows past farmland and a town. (a) State how you could show the treated water is not pure water. (b) Name two pollutants that might be found in the river and their sources.
items.answer: (a) Its boiling point would be slightly above 100 °C (or m.p. below 0 °C); evaporation leaves a residue. (b) Nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers; sewage from the town; metal compounds from industry; plastics from litter.

items.stem: Arjun visits a water-treatment works that supplies drinking water to a large city. (a) Describe the stages in treating the water to make it safe to drink, giving the purpose of each. (b) Suggest why chlorine is added at the end of the process.
items.answer: (a) Sedimentation and filtration — remove solids; carbon — removes tastes/odours; chlorination — kills microbes. (b) To kill microbes so the water stays safe in the pipes to homes.

items.stem: Leila visits a water-treatment works that supplies drinking water to a large city. (a) Describe a chemical test for water. (b) State how you could show the treated water is not pure water. (c) Name two pollutants that might be found in the river and their sources.
items.answer: (a) Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns white to blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride blue to pink). (b) Its boiling point would be slightly above 100 °C (or m.p. below 0 °C); evaporation leaves a residue. (c) Nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers; sewage from the town; metal compounds from industry; plastics from litter.

items.stem: Which three elements are supplied by NPK fertilisers?
items.answer: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
items.markingKey: N, P, K are the main elements needed for plant growth.

items.stem: Explain why farmers should not spread lime (calcium hydroxide) on soil at the same time as ammonium fertilisers.
items.answer: The alkali reacts with ammonium salts to release ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost from the soil.

items.stem: Explain why a farmer might choose ammonium phosphate rather than ammonium nitrate.
items.answer: Ammonium phosphate supplies both nitrogen and phosphorus, whereas ammonium nitrate supplies only nitrogen.

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄.
Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄.

Chloe prepares a sample of ammonium nitrate in the laboratory by titrating aqueous ammonia with nitric acid. (a) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate. (b) Explain why this fertiliser should not be mixed with calcium hydroxide.
items.answer: (a) 35.0% (b) Calcium hydroxide is an alkali; it reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, losing nitrogen.

items.stem: Explain how overuse of fertilisers can harm rivers.
items.answer: Excess soluble nitrates are washed into rivers, causing eutrophication and loss of oxygen for aquatic life.

items.stem: Explain why fertilisers must be soluble in water.
items.answer: Plants absorb the ions in solution through their roots.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why fertilisers must be soluble in water. (b) Explain why a farmer might choose ammonium phosphate rather than ammonium nitrate.
items.answer: (a) Plants absorb the ions in solution through their roots. (b) Ammonium phosphate supplies both nitrogen and phosphorus, whereas ammonium nitrate supplies only nitrogen.

items.stem: Ammonium sulfate is made by reacting ammonia with sulfuric acid: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium sulfate that can be made from 170 tonnes of ammonia.
items.answer: 660 tonnes
items.markingKey: n(NH₃) = 170/17 = 10.0 (k)mol [1]; ratio 2:1 so n(salt) = 5.00 [1]; Mr = 132, mass = 660 tonnes [1]

items.stem: Ammonium nitrate is made by reacting ammonia with nitric acid: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonium nitrate that can be made from 68 tonnes of ammonia.
items.answer: 320 tonnes
items.markingKey: n(NH₃) = 68/17 = 4.00 (k)mol [1]; ratio 1:1 so n(salt) = 4.00 [1]; Mr = 80, mass = 320 tonnes [1]

items.stem: Amara prepares a sample of ammonium phosphate in the laboratory by titrating aqueous ammonia with phosphoric acid. (a) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium phosphate. (b) Explain why this fertiliser should not be mixed with calcium hydroxide.
items.answer: (a) 28.2% (b) Calcium hydroxide is an alkali; it reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, losing nitrogen.

items.stem: A farmer buys 40 kg bags of ammonium nitrate fertiliser for a wheat field. (a) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate. (b) Explain why this fertiliser should not be mixed with calcium hydroxide. (c) State which other element(s) a farmer might need to add, and suggest a compound to supply it.
items.answer: (a) 35.0% (b) Calcium hydroxide is an alkali; it reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, losing nitrogen. (c) Potassium (e.g. potassium nitrate/sulfate) and phosphorus (e.g. ammonium phosphate).

items.stem: What is the approximate percentage of oxygen in clean, dry air?
items.markingKey: Air: about 78% N₂, 21% O₂, small amounts of noble gases (mainly Ar) and CO₂.

items.stem: Explain how oxides of nitrogen are formed in a car engine.
items.answer: At the very high temperature in the engine, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together.

items.stem: Explain how sulfur dioxide causes damage to limestone buildings.
items.answer: SO₂ dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone.

items.stem: Calculate the volume of argon in a room containing 2400 dm³ of clean, dry air.
items.answer: 21.6 dm³

items.stem: 80 cm³ of air is passed repeatedly over heated copper in a sealed apparatus until the volume stops changing. The final volume (at room temperature) is 63.2 cm³. Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air and explain why the copper turns black.
items.answer: 21.0%; the copper reacts with oxygen to form black copper(II) oxide.

items.stem: A report compares the air in a quiet rural village with the air in a busy industrial city. (a) Explain one harmful effect of sulfur dioxide. (b) Explain how carbon monoxide is linked to the source you would expect near a busy road.
items.answer: (a) Acid rain, which damages buildings and kills trees and aquatic life. (b) Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels; traffic burns large amounts of fuel.

items.stem: Which gas makes up about 78% of clean, dry air?
items.answer: nitrogen
items.markingKey: Nitrogen is the main component of air.

items.stem: Explain why incomplete combustion is more likely in a poorly ventilated room.
items.answer: There is not enough oxygen, so carbon fuels form carbon monoxide and soot instead of carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Explain why particulates are harmful to human health.
items.answer: Fine particles are breathed deep into the lungs, increasing respiratory problems and the risk of cancer.

items.stem: Approximately what volume of oxygen is present in 250 dm³ of clean, dry air?
items.answer: 52.5 dm³

items.stem: Coal containing 2.5% sulfur by mass is burned. Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced from 100 tonnes of the coal. (S + O₂ → SO₂)
items.answer: 5.00 tonnes
items.markingKey: mass S = 2.5/100 × 100 = 2.50 t [1]; 32 t S gives 64 t SO₂, so mass SO₂ = 5.00 t [1]

items.stem: Coal containing 0.5% sulfur by mass is burned. Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced from 500 tonnes of the coal. (S + O₂ → SO₂)
items.answer: 5.00 tonnes
items.markingKey: mass S = 0.5/100 × 500 = 2.50 t [1]; 32 t S gives 64 t SO₂, so mass SO₂ = 5.00 t [1]

items.stem: Which two gases are the main greenhouse gases linked to climate change?
items.answer: carbon dioxide and methane
items.markingKey: CO₂ and CH₄ absorb and re-emit thermal (infrared) energy.

items.stem: Explain how increased greenhouse gas emissions lead to climate change.
items.answer: More CO₂/CH₄ absorbs and re-emits more thermal energy towards Earth, raising average temperatures, which changes weather patterns, melts ice and raises sea levels.

items.stem: Explain why planting trees can help reduce climate change.
items.answer: Trees remove carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis.

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction when sulfur dioxide is removed by calcium oxide.
items.answer: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction when the catalytic converter removes carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide together.
items.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction when nitrogen monoxide is converted back to its elements in a catalytic converter.
items.answer: 2NO → N₂ + O₂

items.stem: Grace reads a report about rising carbon dioxide and methane levels in the atmosphere. (a) Name two pollutants removed by a catalytic converter. (b) Explain why catalytic converters do not reduce climate change.
items.answer: (a) Carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen (also unburned hydrocarbons). (b) They convert CO to CO₂, which is still a greenhouse gas.

items.stem: A city council plans to cut air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions over the next ten years. (a) State two effects of climate change. (b) Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis and explain how it affects the atmosphere.
items.answer: (a) Rising sea levels; melting ice caps; more extreme weather; changes in rainfall/crop growth; flooding; droughts. (b) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; it removes CO₂ and adds O₂.

items.stem: Which reaction occurs in a catalytic converter?
items.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂
items.markingKey: Pt/Rh catalyst: carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide react to form carbon dioxide and nitrogen.

items.stem: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
items.answer: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

items.stem: Explain why catalytic converters work only once the engine is warm.
items.answer: The catalyst needs a high temperature to work effectively.

items.stem: Explain why using hydrogen as a fuel in cars reduces pollution, but may not stop all CO₂ emissions.
items.answer: Burning hydrogen gives only water; but hydrogen is often made using energy from fossil fuels.

items.stem: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide needed to make 180 g of glucose by photosynthesis. 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in kg, released when 5 kg of ethanol burns completely. C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
items.markingKey: Mr C₂H₅OH = 46 [1]; 1 mol fuel → 2 mol CO₂ [1]; mass = 5 × 2 × 44/46 = 9.57 kg [1]

items.stem: A plant makes 360 g of glucose by photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide removed from the air at r.t.p., in dm³, and the mass of oxygen released.

items.stem: Hana reads a report about rising carbon dioxide and methane levels in the atmosphere. (a) Explain how carbon dioxide causes the Earth’s temperature to rise. (b) Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis and explain how it affects the atmosphere.
items.answer: (a) It absorbs thermal (infrared) energy emitted by the Earth and re-emits it, some back towards the surface. (b) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; it removes CO₂ and adds O₂.

items.stem: Why is chlorine added to the domestic water supply?
items.answer: To kill microbes

items.stem: Explain why untreated sewage in drinking water is dangerous.
items.answer: It contains harmful microbes that cause diseases such as cholera.

items.stem: A government in Toronto is considering two policies: planting trees and reducing livestock farming. Explain how each would reduce pollution or climate change.
